items.title: Oriented surface and positive quarter-turn
items.statement: For an oriented Riemannian 2-manifold define J_p as the unique g-isometry with J_p²=-I and (v,J_pv) positive for each nonzero v; J is smooth and is reversed when the surface orientation is reversed.
items.strategy: Use an oriented orthonormal frame to set J(E₁)=E₂ and J(E₂)=-E₁; check that this formula is invariant under SO(2) changes of frame and is smooth.

items.title: Connection form of an oriented orthonormal frame
items.statement: For any local positively oriented orthonormal frame (E₁,E₂), define the smooth one-form ω by ω(X)=g(∇_X E₁,E₂). Metric compatibility gives ∇_X E₁=ω(X)E₂ and ∇_X E₂=-ω(X)E₁; this convention is the negative of the Lee/Datar connection form.
items.strategy: Use affine-connection linearity and smoothness to check that ω is a one-form, then differentiate g(E_i,E_j)=δ_ij to derive both frame equations. Compare signs explicitly with Lee and Datar, who define ω_std(X)=g(E₁,∇_X E₂)=-ω(X).

references.title: John M. Lee, Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature (1997)
references.locator: Chapter 9, §The Gauss–Bonnet Formula, printed p. 165 (PDF p. 181), lines 6471–6488: Lee defines ω_std(X)=g(E₁,∇_X E₂)=-g(∇_X E₁,E₂), giving ∇_X E₁=-ω_std(X)E₂ and ∇_X E₂=ω_std(X)E₁. The convention in this item is ω=-ω_std.

references.locator: Lecture 2, §2.1, printed p. 11 (PDF p. 18), lines 604–615: Datar defines ω_std(X)=g(E₁,∇_X E₂)=-g(∇_X E₁,E₂) and records the resulting frame equations. The convention in this item is ω=-ω_std.

items.title: Rotation law for the surface connection form
items.statement: Let $(M,g)$ be an oriented Riemannian surface and $U\subseteq M$ open with specified smooth positively oriented $g$-orthonormal frames $(E_1,E_2)$ and $(E'_1,E'_2)$, with connection forms $\omega$ and $\omega'$ in the convention $\omega(X)=g(\nabla_XE_1,E_2)$. On each open patch $V\subseteq U$ where a smooth angle lift $\varphi:V\to\mathbb R$ is supplied with $E'_1=\cos\varphi E_1+\sin\varphi E_2$ and $E'_2=-\sin\varphi E_1+\cos\varphi E_2$, the forms satisfy $\omega'|_V=\omega|_V+d\varphi$, where $d\varphi(X)=X(\varphi)$. Any two such lifts of the same frame rotation differ by a locally constant element of $2\pi\mathbb Z$, so their differentials agree on overlaps; no global angle lift is asserted.
items.strategy: Differentiate E'_1 in an arbitrary direction X using the declared frame equations and dφ(X)=Xφ. Collect the E_1 and E_2 coefficients to obtain ∇_X E'_1=(ω(X)+Xφ)E'_2, then take its inner product with the unit vector E'_2. For two lifts of the same rotation, equality of sine and cosine implies their difference lies in 2πZ; continuity makes it locally constant, so the differential identity agrees on connected overlaps even when no global lift exists.

references.locator: Chapter 9, §The Gauss–Bonnet Formula, printed p. 165 (PDF p. 181), equations (9.4), lines 6471–6488: Lee's frame equations use ω_std(X)=g(E₁,∇_X E₂)=−ω(X) relative to this pair. The frame-rotation identity is derived directly in the item, not attributed to this passage.

items.title: Gaussian curvature structure equation
items.statement: With R(X,Y)Z=∇_X∇_YZ-∇_Y∇_XZ-∇_[X,Y]Z and K=g(R(E₁,E₂)E₂,E₁), dω=-K dA for the ω defined above.
items.strategy: Compute R(E₁,E₂)E₂=-dω(E₁,E₂)E₁ from the two frame equations and dω(X,Y)=Xω(Y)-Yω(X)-ω([X,Y]). Since dA(E₁,E₂)=1, the sign follows; AC_ω is inherited only through the published sectional-curvature interface.

items.title: Signed geodesic curvature
items.statement: For a regular C2 unit-speed curve in an oriented Riemannian surface, the coordinate expression A^k = d2x^k/dt2 + Gamma^k_ij (dx^i/dt)(dx^j/dt) is a chart-independent covariant acceleration; for smooth curves it is D_t T, and it extends this formula to C2 curves. Metric compatibility gives g(A,T)=0, so define signed geodesic curvature by A=k_g JT and k_g=g(A,JT). For a unit-speed positively oriented boundary arc JT is the inward unit conormal; for any regular-speed tangent T the inward unit conormal is JT/|T|. Curve-parameter or surface-orientation reversal changes the sign.
items.strategy: Use the affine and along-curve connection rules to identify the coordinate acceleration, then apply the Christoffel transformation law and the second chain rule to prove chart independence for C2 curves. Differentiate g(T,T)=1 using metric compatibility to prove A perpendicular to T, then use the positive orthonormal basis (T,JT) to define its scalar component. Derive the outward-normal-first sign and calculate a counterclockwise Euclidean circle of radius R, for which k_g=1/R; check parameter and surface-orientation reversal.

items.title: Signs of geodesic curvature under reversals
items.statement: Let $(M,g,J)$ be an oriented Riemannian surface and $\gamma:I\to M$ a regular $C^2$ unit-speed curve on an interval $I$ with nonempty interior. Write $k_{J,\gamma}$ for its signed geodesic curvature. Reversing the surface orientation replaces $J$ by $-J$, and for every $s\in I$ gives $k_{-J,\gamma}(s)=-k_{J,\gamma}(s)$. Define $I^{\mathrm{rev}}=-I$ and $\gamma^{\mathrm{rev}}(t)=\gamma(-t)$ for $t\in I^{\mathrm{rev}}$. For every $t\in I^{\mathrm{rev}}$, reversing the curve parameter with $J$ fixed gives $k_{J,\gamma^{\mathrm{rev}}}(t)=-k_{J,\gamma}(-t)$; reversing both the surface orientation and curve parameter gives $k_{-J,\gamma^{\mathrm{rev}}}(t)=k_{J,\gamma}(-t)$. At included endpoints, use one-sided derivatives.
items.strategy: Use the signed-curvature definition $k_{J,\gamma}=g(A_\gamma,JT)$. Replacing $J$ by $-J$ changes only the normal factor. For $\gamma^{\mathrm{rev}}(t)=\gamma(-t)$, compute in a chart that the first derivative changes sign, the second derivative does not, and the quadratic Christoffel term is unchanged; hence $A_{\gamma^{\mathrm{rev}}}(t)=A_\gamma(-t)$ while the unit tangent changes sign. Apply these two sign changes independently and together, with the parameter arguments stated explicitly. Check zero curvature and one-sided endpoints; no choice is used.

items.title: Tangent-angle formula for geodesic curvature
items.statement: Let $(M,g,J)$ be an oriented Riemannian surface, $U\subseteq M$ an open set with a specified smooth positively oriented $g$-orthonormal frame $(E_1,E_2)$, and $\omega(X)=g(\nabla_XE_1,E_2)$ the connection one-form in this convention. items.title: Signed exterior angle at an ordinary corner
items.statement: At an ordinary corner of an oriented surface region, let T₋ and T₊ be the incoming and outgoing unit tangents. The signed exterior angle α is the unique number in (−π,π) with T₊=cos(α)T₋+sin(α)JT₋; opposite tangents are excluded. For a positively oriented convex or reflex boundary corner of interior angle β∈(0,2π), α=π−β.
items.strategy: Use the positive quarter-turn J to form an oriented orthonormal basis (T₋,JT₋); the nonopposite condition gives a unique principal angle. Derive α=π−β from the interior sector on the left of a positively oriented boundary. Check zero/straight angle, cusp exclusion, orientation reversal and parameter reversal explicitly.

items.title: Total turning with connection and corner terms
items.statement: For a closed piecewise smooth regular curve carried by one oriented frame, its tangent-angle rotation is ∫k_g ds-∮ω+Σα. For a cover by frames, transition-angle jumps are included and the same total is frame-independent. For possibly self-intersecting curves the ordinary signed corner turn is defined locally as the unique angle in (-pi,pi) from the incoming unit tangent to the outgoing one in the positive tangent-plane orientation.
items.strategy: Integrate θ′=k_g-ω on every smooth arc, add the signed corner jumps, and telescope. On changing frames, θ changes by the negative rotation angle while ω changes by its differential; their contributions cancel.

items.title: Rotation index of a regular closed plane curve
items.statement: For a closed regular plane curve with matching endpoint tangents, define its rotation index as (θ(b)-θ(a))/(2π), where θ is a lift of the unit-tangent angle; include prescribed jumps for ordinary corners.
items.strategy: Construct each smooth-arc angle lift on a finite subdivision into open semicircle charts, using a Lebesgue number; paste the unique principal corner jumps in (-π,π), then prove the total increment is an integer multiple of 2π and independent of the initial lift.

items.title: Hopf turning-tangent theorem with ordinary corners
items.statement: A positively oriented simple closed piecewise C² regular plane curve that bounds a supplied disk region and has finitely many ordinary corners has ∫k_plane ds+Σα=2π.
items.strategy: For a smooth curve choose a lowest point, lift the normalized secant direction on the parameter triangle and compare its three boundary sides to show one full positive turn. Round each ordinary corner in a disjoint small disk by a simple regular arc whose tangent rotation equals the chosen jump, then pass to the limit. The supplied region avoids appealing to the unproved general Jordan curve remark.

items.title: Regular oriented surface regions with corners
items.statement: A regular oriented region is a compact embedded surface domain whose boundary is a finite union of pairwise disjoint simple closed piecewise-C² curves, with finite cyclic arc decompositions and half-disk charts on smooth arcs and sector charts at vertices. At a vertex the one-sided boundary tangents are not antipodal, excluding the ±π cusp; smooth arcs receive the outward-normal-first orientation, and an empty boundary is allowed. A disk region carries a supplied homeomorphism of pairs from the closed disk and its circle to the region and its boundary.
items.strategy: Use boundary half-charts away from corners and embedded quadrant or reflex-wedge charts at ordinary corners. Specify that the corner set is finite and that an angle of ±π is excluded.

items.title: Stokes formula for finite ordinary surface corners
items.statement: Let M be an oriented smooth surface without boundary, let D⊆M be a compact regular oriented surface region with finitely many ordinary corners, and let η be a smooth 1-form on a neighbourhood of D. Then ∫_D dη=∫_{∂D}η, where the boundary integral is the sum over the finitely many positively oriented C² boundary arcs.
items.strategy: Localize by a finite bump partition in positive interior, smooth-boundary, and corner charts. In interior charts apply compact-support Euclidean Stokes. In boundary charts express the boundary as a C² graph, integrate dη by vertical sections, and use Newton–Leibniz to identify the result with the outward-normal-first line integral. At corners the graph has two C² pieces; split at the vertex and cancel the shared endpoint terms. Compare chart localizations by finite overlap refinement and compactly supported change of variables. Only finite bump choices are used; no choice axiom is needed.

items.title: Finite planar graph disk cuts and Euler count
items.statement: Assume full AC. A finite embedded graph in a closed round disk, with regular edge endpoint germs and pairwise distinct incident tangent rays, can be augmented by polygonal cuts to a connected face-to-face triangular disk decomposition satisfying V-E+F=1.
items.strategy: Use finite polygonal arcs to connect components and reduce the cut-vertex potential. Root an ear decomposition of the resulting 2-connected regular drawing at the disk boundary cycle. Extend the earlier Jordan crosscut region-label proof to its simple nonpolygonal ears using Jordan–Schönflies local sides, thereby proving simple-cycle disk faces and Euler. Insert sequential polygonal face fans, reconcile full-edge intersections, and remove the exterior face from the plane Euler count.

items.title: Finite frameable decomposition of a regular disk region
items.statement: Assume full AC. Every compact regular oriented disk region with ordinary corners admits a finite face-to-face subdivision into frameable regular disk pieces retaining the supplied boundary.
items.strategy: Choose finitely many small oriented coordinate disks whose interiors cover the region, with polygonal boundaries in their charts. On each chart, Gram–Schmidt applied to its positive coordinate frame and the supplied metric gives the required positive orthonormal frame. Perturb the finitely many disk parameters and vertices to make distinct boundary arcs transverse, avoiding coincidence with the supplied boundary; prove the transversality and finiteness from the parameter functions and Morse–Sard rather than assuming general position. Overlay the disk boundaries with the supplied boundary: membership in each covering disk is constant on every complementary component, hence each lies in at least one frameable chart. Apply the local planar graph disk-cut lemma to split holes and non-disk components by finitely many arcs. The finite resulting disk cells are face-to-face, and no general Jordan theorem or plane-graph page is consumed.

items.title: Local Gauss–Bonnet on a framed disk region
items.statement: Assume full AC. A compact regular oriented frameable disk region with ordinary corners satisfies integral K dA plus boundary integral kg ds plus signed exterior angles equals 2pi.
items.strategy: Subdivide the disk into finitely many chart-contained triangular disks. In each disk compare a smooth frame with the coordinate frame using a rotation lift on that disk, compute its turning by metric interpolation and the plane turning theorem, then use the angle derivative formula, structure equation and corner Stokes. Cancel internal edge integrals; count corner angles with the finite regular CW Euler identity. Full AC enters through the decomposition and its planar suppliers.

items.strategy: Each geodesic side has k_g=0, while its exterior jump is π minus its interior angle. Substitute the three jumps into the framed-disk formula.

items.title: Curvilinear face-to-face triangulation
items.statement: A curvilinear triangulation of a compact smooth surface (possibly disconnected, nonorientable, or with boundary) is a finite face-to-face decomposition by embedded closed triangular disk regions. Each face has a disk parametrization, three distinct vertices, three distinct piecewise C² regular edges and ordinary corners; faces meet only in a common full edge, common vertex, or not at all. Interior edges have two incident faces, boundary edges lie in ∂M and have one; the face sectors at a vertex form a circle in the interior or an interval at the boundary. The union is M and ∂M is the boundary-edge subcomplex; each vertex, edge and face is counted once.
items.strategy: Define the finite vertex, edge and face incidence data, the homeomorphism from each closed standard triangle, and local regular-region charts along edges and corners. Require the finite links to be circles or boundary intervals and the face incidences to match the manifold boundary. Orient each face only by its reference triangle; do not impose a global orientation. Prescribed boundary edges are arbitrary regular boundary arcs and need not be geodesics.

references.title: Jürgen Jost, Compact Riemann Surfaces: An Introduction to Contemporary Mathematics
references.locator: §2.3.A, Definition 2.3.A.1, printed pp. 31–32 (PDF pp. 43–44), lines 1776–1793: finite triangular subsets, a homeomorphism from a planar triangle for each face, and pairwise disjoint/common-vertex/common-full-edge intersections. This is topological and treats closed surfaces; the piecewise-C² and boundary conditions here are separately specified.

items.title: Geodesic triangulation with prescribed boundary arcs
items.statement: A geodesic triangulation of a compact Riemannian surface (M,g) is a supplied curvilinear triangulation such that each edge e not contained in ∂M admits a regular C² embedding γ:[0,1]→M with image e, with γ((0,1))⊂Int M and γ|_(0,1) a geodesic for (Int M,g|Int M) with its Levi–Civita connection. Edges contained in ∂M are prescribed regular C² boundary arcs and need not be geodesics. The condition asks for an affine geodesic parametrization of each nonboundary edge; it imposes no length-minimizing requirement and asserts no existence of such a triangulation.
items.strategy: Audit the distinction between edges contained in the boundary and edges whose relative interiors lie in the interior; include edges that end on the boundary in the latter case. Use the Levi–Civita connection of the restricted metric on the boundaryless open submanifold Int M, and require an affine geodesic parametrization only on (0,1). Keep the supplied regular C² extension at endpoints, allow arbitrary prescribed regular C² boundary arcs, and make no minimization or existence claim.

It does not require geodesic edges; this is contextual only.

items.title: Extending a compact surface metric across its boundary
items.statement: Assume AC_ω. For a compact smooth surface M with boundary and a smooth Riemannian metric g on M, the metric on either labelled copy extends to a smooth Riemannian metric on an open neighbourhood of that copy in the smooth double DM.
items.strategy: Use the published smooth-double and local tensor-extension results. At each seam point, symmetrize a local extension of g and shrink its neighbourhood until it is positive definite. Compactness of the seam gives finitely many such neighbourhoods. On their union, patch the positive extensions with a smooth partition of unity on the double; every local extension equals g on the original half, so the convex sum does too. Glue this patched metric to g on the open interior of the original copy. AC_ω is used by the published double and partition suppliers; the finite subcover and finite extension selections use only finite choice.

references.title: Panagiotis Polymerakis, On the spectrum of differential operators under Riemannian coverings
references.locator: Section 3, Lemma 3.2, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 12): extend metric components locally, shrink until positive definite, and patch extensions with a partition of unity. The paper uses an attached boundary cylinder rather than the labelled double used here.

items.title: Uniform short-geodesic scale on a compact surface
items.statement: Assume AC_ω. Let K be either a compact smooth Riemannian surface with smooth boundary, identified with a labelled copy in its smooth double and supplied with the open metric-extension neighbourhood N, or a compact regular oriented surface region with ordinary corners in a supplied boundaryless ambient Riemannian surface N. With d_N the componentwise Riemannian distance, if K is nonempty there are finitely many strongly geodesically convex open sets V_i covering K and r>0 such that every p,q∈K with d_N(p,q)<3r lie together in some V_i and have a unique affinely parametrized ambient length-minimizing geodesic there, of length d_N(p,q). The connector is constant when p=q. For empty K use the empty cover. Smooth boundary points retain one-sided collar neighborhoods in the double; cornered regions use supplied half-disk and wedge charts. Ambient connectors need not remain in K, and any later finite network must retain the supplied smooth boundary arcs as prescribed edges.
items.strategy: In the smooth-boundary case, use the metric-extension lemma to work in a boundaryless open Riemannian neighbourhood in the double; a cornered region already lies in its boundaryless ambient surface. Split compact K across the finitely many ambient components meeting it. In each component the Riemannian distance induces the manifold topology, so the closed component pieces of K are compact metric spaces. Consider the set of all strongly geodesically convex open neighborhoods contained in an ambient component; the relative convex-neighborhood theorem supplies one around each point. Take a finite subcover and apply the Lebesgue-number lemma on each compact component piece. A positive r below one third of the least Lebesgue number ensures every pair at distance below 3r lies in a common V_i; strong convexity gives its unique affine globally minimizing connector. By the definition of componentwise distance as the infimum of piecewise-C¹ competitor lengths, the connector length is d_N(p,q)<3r. Collars and corner charts are domain-side data; retain original boundary arcs as prescribed edges in every later network.

items.title: Finite curvilinear triangulation of a compact Riemannian surface
items.statement: Assume full AC. Every compact smooth Riemannian surface, with smooth boundary allowed, has a finite regular C2 face-to-face curvilinear triangulation preserving its boundary and subordinate to any supplied finite strongly convex ambient cover; a regular cornered region has analogous triangular face/edge/link data with ordinary corners. Its finite regular CW count V-E+F is the homology Euler characteristic.
items.strategy: Choose generic small metric-circle arrangement, assign each face one larger normal-coordinate disk, apply the regular positive-sector planar fan lemma, reconcile edge subdivisions, smooth polygonal bends, and identify the finite CW count.

items.statement: Assume full AC. Finely subdivide every interior edge and replace each subarc by its minimizing geodesic chord. Uniform O(h²) position and O(h) tangent estimates, positive vertex sectors, separation away from vertices, and inward boundary sectors preserve an embedded graph with the same disk faces and shared edges. Keep boundary arcs fixed.

items.title: A curvilinear triangulation gives a finite CW structure
items.statement: The open vertices, relative interiors of edges, and interiors of faces of a finite face-to-face curvilinear triangulation of a compact surface form a finite regular CW complex. Its characteristic maps are homeomorphisms from closed balls onto the corresponding closed cells, and its 0-, 1-, and 2-cells are indexed respectively by V, E, and F.
items.strategy: Build the 0-, 1-, and 2-skeleta by attaching the supplied vertices, edge intervals, and triangular disks along their stated endpoints and full-edge boundaries. The face-to-face clauses give the attaching maps and disjoint open cells. Prove closure-finiteness from the finite inventory and the weak topology from the finite closed cover; compact interval and face images are closed in the Hausdorff surface. Verify regularity from the supplied embeddings and disk homeomorphisms. Do not invoke Euler–Poincaré or a metric-comparison result: this lemma only identifies the finite cell structure and its counts.

items.title: The Gauss–Bonnet curvature and boundary expression is metric independent
items.statement: Assume full AC. The Gauss-Bonnet curvature/boundary/corner expression for a fixed regular oriented region, and the total curvature density for a fixed closed nonorientable surface, are independent of metric.
items.strategy: Interpolate g_t=(1−t)g₀+tg₁. On a finite disk cover, apply the positive g₀-to-g_t square-root bundle map to a fixed oriented g₀-frame; the resulting g_t-frames have the same SO(2) transition functions for all t. Hence β=ω₁−ω₀ glues to a global 1-form in the oriented case, and dω=−K dA gives K₁dA₁−K₀dA₀=−dβ. Stokes makes the curvature-integral change −∫∂Mβ. Along each fixed regular boundary arc, the angle formula gives (k₁ds₁−k₀ds₀)=d(θ₁−θ₀)+β. The angle difference has a single-valued lift through the metric path; its total derivative over closed boundary components plus its finite corner jumps is zero. Each corner jump difference is exactly α₁−α₀, so the boundary and corner change is +∫∂Mβ and cancels. On a closed nonorientable surface use a fixed finite disk triangulation from the first metric, choose each face orientation separately, perform the same β computation on its faces, and pair interior-edge integrals: reversal of face orientation changes both β and its integration orientation, leaving opposite inward conormals and cancellation. No classification, Euler–Poincaré theorem or later characteristic-form theory is used.

items.title: Topological well-definedness of the surface Euler characteristic
items.statement: Every supplied finite curvilinear triangulation of a compact smooth surface has V-E+F equal to its singular-homology Euler characteristic, independent of metric, orientation, boundary, and triangulation.
items.strategy: For one fixed metric, apply the local disk formula to every face of either piecewise C² curvilinear triangulation; geodesicity of interior edges is unnecessary because their signed geodesic-curvature integrals cancel. The face-edge and angle count of the supplied summation lemma yields V−E+F=G_g(M)/(2π), where G includes the boundary and corner terms, or the curvature density for closed nonorientable M. The direct cell-structure lemma confirms that V,E,F count the same kinds of finite cells. For different metrics, apply the preceding local metric-transgression lemma to identify their G values. Thus the two counts agree without a common subdivision of unrelated smooth arcs or the out-of-closure cellular-homology page.

items.statement: Assume full AC. For R²/Z² with its descended Euclidean metric, K=0 and χ=0, so Gauss–Bonnet reads 0=0.

items.statement: Assume AC. On the radius-R round sphere, a simple geodesic triangle of area A has angle sum π+A/R²; a spherical octant has A=πR²/2 and three right angles.

items.title: Spherical cap boundary sign
items.statement: Assume full AC. For the north polar cap 0≤θ≤θ₀<π on a radius-R sphere, ∫K dA=2π(1-cos θ₀) and its positive boundary has ∫k_g ds=2π cos θ₀, summing to 2π.
items.strategy: In polar coordinates on a radius-R sphere, compute K=R⁻², cap area 2πR²(1−cos θ₀), and boundary length 2πRsin θ₀. The positively oriented latitude has inward conormal toward decreasing θ and k_g=cot θ₀/R, so its integral is 2πcos θ₀. The sum is 2π=2πχ(D), and the sign is fixed by the outward-normal-first convention. These metric computations are made here.

items.statement: In a closed tetrahedral combinatorial pattern V=4,E=6,F=4, the four vertex angle sums contribute 8π and 3F=2E, leaving 2π(V-E+F)=4π in the local-to-global count; this is a finite bookkeeping check only.

items.title: Projective-plane curvature via a hemisphere
items.statement: Assume full AC. The round real projective plane obtained by antipodal identification has K=1/R², area=2πR² and χ=1; hence its total curvature is 2π.
items.strategy: Construct RP² directly as the unit sphere modulo x∼−x; a small spherical disk disjoint from its antipodal image projects isometrically, so the quotient carries the round metric without invoking a covering theorem. A hemisphere meets each antipodal pair once except for the equator, which has area zero; thus its total curvature is half of 4π, namely 2π. The nonorientable theorem then gives χ(RP²)=1. Compute K=1 and the sphere area in polar coordinates within this example.

items.statement: Assume full AC. On a Euclidean disk, replacing outward-normal-first by inward-normal-first makes the boundary clockwise and changes ∫k_g ds from +2π to -2π while χ=1.
items.strategy: Compute JT for the clockwise unit tangent in the fixed surface orientation and find k_g=-1/R. The resulting -2π cannot satisfy the outward-normal-first Gauss–Bonnet identity.

items.title: A deformed sphere has the same total curvature
items.statement: Assume full AC. Any smooth positive metric on the underlying oriented sphere, including the induced metric of an ellipsoid, has total Gaussian curvature 4π although its pointwise curvature need not be constant.
items.strategy: The preceding round-sphere example computes χ=2. Apply metric independence to any other smooth metric on the same oriented sphere, giving total curvature 4π. For a nonspherical ellipsoid, unequal principal radii at different axes show its induced K varies, so constancy of the integral is substantive.
